title: Levers, Pulleys and Gears
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Levers, Pulleys and Gears Worksheets (Mechanisms and Forces)
standard_text: Recognise that some mechanisms, including levers, pulleys and gears, allow a smaller force to have a greater effect.
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on levers, pulleys and gears: pivots and balancing, pulley ropes and effort, gear teeth and turns, and everyday mechanisms. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A small force, a big effect.
key_sub: Longer levers, more pulley ropes and the right gears all reduce the effort.
body_html:
How to think about it

Levers, pulleys and gears let a small force have a bigger effect.

  • Lever: effort × distance = load × distance. Push further from the pivot to lift more easily.
  • Pulleys: a single pulley changes direction; more supporting ropes share the load (effort = load ÷ ropes).
  • Gears: touching gears turn opposite ways; a small gear driving a big gear turns more times.
Example

Load 120 N at 1 m, effort at 3 m?

120 × 1 ÷ 3

Answer: 40 N

Example

10-tooth gear drives 30-tooth gear. Turns of small for 1 big?

30 ÷ 10

Answer: 3 turns

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a longer lever needs more effort.
  • Thinking a pulley makes the load lighter.
  • Thinking touching gears turn the same way.

faq.q: How does a lever make lifting easier?
faq.a: Pushing further from the pivot means a smaller force can lift a heavier load. Effort × distance from pivot = load × distance from pivot.
A single pulley changes the direction of the pull. A system with more ropes holding the load shares it, so less effort is needed (but you pull more rope).

faq.q: Why do gears turn in opposite directions?
faq.a: Their teeth push against each other, so when one gear turns clockwise, the gear it touches turns anticlockwise.
